title: Maximal-minor integral differences for Lipschitz perturbations

content.display_title: Maximal-minor integral differences for Lipschitz perturbations
content.one_sentence_role: Passes the smooth compact-perturbation identity to Lipschitz maps through local strong convergence.
content.natural_language_statement:
Fix $n\geq1$ and $g,u:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^N$ be globally Lipschitz, with $u$ compactly supported. Fix a set of $n$ output indices $s=\{s_1<\cdots<s_n\}$. Define $\pi_s(y)=(y_{s_1},\ldots,y_{s_n})$ and the signed selected minor
$$M_s(f)(x)=\det(\pi_s\circ Df(x)).$$
Then
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n}\bigl(M_s(g+u)(x)-M_s(g)(x)\bigr)\,dx=0.$$
content.assumptions:
There are finite constants $C_g,C_u\geq0$ such that, for all $x,y$,
$$\|g(x)-g(y)\|_\infty\leq C_g\|x-y\|_\infty,\qquad
\|u(x)-u(y)\|_\infty\leq C_u\|x-y\|_\infty.$$
The support convention is $\operatorname{supp}u:=\overline{\{x:u(x)\ne0\}}$, and only this set must be compact. The fixed selection $s$ consists of $n$ distinct output coordinates in increasing order, so its existence entails $N\geq n$. Differentiability everywhere and a boundary condition are not assumed.
content.conclusion: The same signed minor $M_s$ occurs in both terms, and their difference is integrable with integral zero. No absolute value is placed around either determinant, and separate whole-space integrability of the two minors is not claimed.
content.proof_summary: Smooth both maps, use one compact set for all small-parameter perturbations, pass each restricted determinant integral to the limit, and finally identify the whole-space difference.

proof_steps.text:
The support lemma provides a compact $K$ containing $\operatorname{supp}u$ and also $\operatorname{supp}u_\varepsilon$ for every sufficiently small positive $\varepsilon$. Lipschitz maps are locally integrable, so mollification is linear: $(g+u)_\varepsilon=g_\varepsilon+u_\varepsilon$. These mollifications are $C^\infty$. Apply the smooth compact-perturbation theorem to $\pi_s\circ g_\varepsilon$ and $\pi_s\circ u_\varepsilon$; output selection preserves compact support. The chain rule identifies their derivatives with selected square operators and gives
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n}\bigl(M_s((g+u)_\varepsilon)-M_s(g_\varepsilon)\bigr)=0.$$

Outside $K$, $u_\varepsilon$ is locally zero. The two maps then agree on a neighborhood, so their derivatives, and thus their selected minors, agree there. The previous integral therefore equals its restriction to $K$. This argument only needs local equality; it does not require differentiability of the unsmoothed maps at every point.

Apply strong local convergence of mollified derivatives to $f=g+u$ and to $f=g$, on this same compact $K$. For $T_s(A)=\pi_s\circ A$, contractivity and linearity give
$$\|T_s(Df_\varepsilon)-T_s(Df)\|_{L^n(K)}\leq\|Df_\varepsilon-Df\|_{L^n(K)}\longrightarrow0.$$
Continuous linear postcomposition preserves eventual $L^n$ membership; the limiting derivative belongs to $L^n(K)$ by its Lipschitz bound. Thus all hypotheses of determinant-integral continuity hold with measure restricted to $K$. Its output is $\int_KM_s(f_\varepsilon)\to\int_KM_s(f)$ for each of these two maps.

The smooth selected minors are integrable on compact $K$. For the limiting maps $f=g+u,g$, the bound $|M_s(f)(x)|\leq n\|\pi_s\circ Df(x)\|_{\mathrm{op}}^n$ and $Df\in L^n(K)$ give the same integrability. Thus both terms may be integrated separately on $K$. Using Step 3 for each term,
$$\begin{aligned}
0&=\int_K\bigl(M_s((g+u)_\varepsilon)-M_s(g_\varepsilon)\bigr)\\
 &=\int_K M_s((g+u)_\varepsilon)-\int_K M_s(g_\varepsilon)\\
 &\longrightarrow\int_K M_s(g+u)-\int_K M_s(g)
 =\int_K\bigl(M_s(g+u)-M_s(g)\bigr).
\end{aligned}$$
This proves the restricted difference integral is zero; it does not subtract unrestricted whole-space integrals.

Outside $K$, the original perturbation $u$ is locally zero, so $M_s(g+u)-M_s(g)=0$ there as well. The difference is integrable on $K$ and equals zero outside; it is therefore integrable on the whole space and has the same integral. This proves the asserted whole-space identity without requiring mollification to preserve any boundary values.

content.lean_realization_notes: The coordinate projection $\pi_s$ is contractive for the sup norms. Postcomposition $A\mapsto\pi_s\circ A$ is a continuous linear map on operator spaces, preserves subtraction, and has norm at most one. Its determinant equals the maximal minor of the standard matrix in precisely the increasing row order.
